facts.fact: Most healthy adult fish can go about a week without food, or two weeks at most.
Almost every fish except newly hatched fry can go 2–3 days, such as a weekend, without being fed.
For trips of a week or less, the simplest option is to skip feeding. Healthy fish can go a week or more without food, depending on species.
While the owner is away, overfeeding is the main danger: uneaten food fouls the water and no one is there to change it.
Herbivores, small active fish and baby fish need food every day or two. Large, older or carnivorous fish need to eat less often.
Newly hatched fish may need 3–8 meals a day. Fish that are active, newly hatched or kept in warm water need feeding more often, even on a short trip.
This Vietnamese retailer gives 3–7 days as the general fasting range for large fish and 2–3 days for juveniles. It says algae eaters such as plecos get hungry sooner than fish eaters.
The same retailer gives these maximum fasting times: betta 7–14 days, guppy 7–10 days, angelfish 7 days, discus 14 days, arowana 21 days.
Fish in a healthy tank with enough oxygen can go roughly 1–2 weeks without food.
Do not add new fish or make major changes to the tank within a month of a long trip.
About one week before a longer trip, change 25% of the water and clean the filter, without disturbing the substrate or the biological media.

Clean the tank 1–2 days before leaving: do a partial water change, vacuum the substrate and clean the filter if needed. Finish about 48 hours before departure so you can confirm fish and equipment are fine.
This source says to change about 70% of the water and clean the tank the day before leaving.
Feed regularly for about a week before leaving, then stop feeding 1 day before departure.
Before leaving, check that the heater works and holds the right temperature.
Put the light on a timer that matches the tank's normal day/night cycle.
Test an automatic feeder for several days before leaving to confirm it works and gives the right amount. Load only enough food for the trip.
Set an automatic feeder to the minimum amount your fish need. It keeps dispensing even if fish stop eating or the filter fails, which can foul the water.
For a sitter, portion each day's food in advance, for example in a pill box or labeled bags. Frozen food cubes are cleaner and easier to portion than flakes.
Have a sitter visit every 2–3 days. Leave buckets of treated water for top-offs, mark the fill levels, and leave your number plus an experienced aquarist's or shop's number.
Keep a sitter's job simple: check the tank, feed, and check the water level. Give written instructions.
Picky eaters on longer trips can be given live foods such as blackworms, daphnia, scuds or snails, kept in a floating container with holes that let the food escape slowly.
After returning from a week or more away, do a water change within a few days. Also check the heater, confirm the filter is flowing and rinse fiber pads.
After returning, check that the fish are healthy and active. Increase feeding gradually over the first 3–5 days and change about 20% of the water.
Run a second filter pump alongside the air pump in case the main pump fails while you are away, and check every filter and air pump before leaving.
A power cut while you are away can cause oxygen shortage and disease, especially if the water was already fouled by heavy feeding.
For absences over 7–10 days, use a good filter and an air pump. A timer switch or phone-app remote control can help manage it.
Aquarium Co-Op advises against vacation feeder blocks: they break into particles larger fish can't eat and can cause ammonia spikes and algae blooms.
Vacation feeder blocks are low in nutrition, can foul the water and may be ignored by the fish. The article calls them risky.
Aqueon says that if you use a feeder block, test it a week before leaving to make sure the fish eat it, and stop all other feeding while it is in use.
Don't starve fish through a trip if they are fry that need daily meals, if they are recovering from illness, or if you'll be gone more than a week.
Sitters who don't know aquariums often overfeed because the fish seem hungry. If a feeding is missed, skip it rather than doubling up later.
Forgetting to switch the filter back on after the pre-trip water change is a common mistake.
Do not clean heavily or disturb the substrate or biological filter media just before a trip.
Don't ask novice sitters to scrape algae, change CO2 cylinders or hatch brine shrimp.
Feeding fish until full the day before leaving fouls the water quickly.
Feeding a lot on return to make up for missed meals can cause digestive problems and bloating. Start with very small portions.
Adding too much live food or too many plants before leaving can dirty the water.
A common Vietnamese worry is caring for the tank while going home to the countryside for Tết (về quê ăn Tết).
For outdoor tanks or styrofoam boxes, duckweed and plants can serve as natural food. Bo bo (Daphnia) or trùn worms can be left as live food that survives in the tank.
Place the tank somewhere well ventilated, away from direct sun and strong heat.
A feeding ring (phễu) with a small amount of tubifex worms (trùn chỉ) can feed fish for about 2–3 days.
For predatory or large fish, this source suggests feeding them until full and then adding about 5–6 small live fish as prey. Add only a few, since too many fouls the water.
This Vietnamese source suggests asking someone to look after the tank if you'll be away more than 5 days.
Fish that went hungry while you were away do not need bigger meals on your return. Aquarium Care says extra food can harm them.
Some Vietnamese sources advise feeding fish more in the week before a trip so they build reserves. Aquarium Co-Op and Aqueon do not give this advice.
Professional fish sitters cost $20/hour or more, casual sitters about $10 per visit, automatic feeders about $25–60 and feeder blocks about $2–6 (US prices).
The Aquarium Co-Op automatic feeder can feed up to 4 times a day, and its battery lasts 3–6 months per charge.
Basic automatic feeders dispense every 12 hours. Better models let you set feeding times. Have someone check the feeder every few days.
This source says to leave the tank light on so fish can find food. US makers instead recommend a light timer that keeps the normal day/night cycle.
